newsitem.title: USA: Normandy founder charged in IPO, bank fraud.
newsitem.headline: Normandy founder charged in IPO, bank fraud.

text.p: Normandy America Inc founder Christopher Bagdasarian, 31, was charged with fraud Thursday in connection with the August 1995 initial public offering of the reinsurance company and for allegedly lying to Chase Manhattan Corp predecessor Chemical Bank to obtain $24.55 million in loans.
The charges accuse Bagdasarian and a former partner at Deloitte & Touche LLP of providing false information in last year's offering of Omaha, Neb.-based Normandy America.
The initial public offering was pulled from the Nasdaq market on August 16, 1995, after one day of trading.
Lead underwriter Salomon Inc had said at the time that the IPO was withdrawn due to market conditions.

Bagdasarian had stated in his U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing prior to last year's IPO that he had been managing money for 10 years, providing his investors with an annualized return of 29 percent.
He said that he began with $37 million in 1984 and ended up managing more than $700 million. This would have meant the defendant had $37 million when he was 19 years old.
Bagdasarian was named in an eight-count criminal complaint filed by the Manhattan U.S. attorney's office and during a court hearing waived his right to an indictment by a federal grand jury.

His lawyer Michael Armstrong would not comment on whether Bagdasarian would later plead guilty to the charges, as sometimes happens when a defendant is charged in a complaint rather than by indictment.
If convicted, he faces up to 165 years in prison and a $5.75 million fine.

Samuel White, 35, of La Canada, Calif., a certified public accountant and former partner in Deloitte & Touche's Los Angeles office, was also named in an eight-count indictment. White, who provided accounting and tax advise to Bagdasarian, faces the same penalties. Both men are accused of conspiracy to commit securities fraud, bank fraud and perjury. They were also sued by the SEC on related civil charges.

Prosecutors allege that the scheme began in February 1992, when Bagdasarian first approached Chemical seeking an $8 million standby letter of credit that he needed for his planned purchase of a Gulfstream IV aircraft.
In connection with his request, he represented himself as a highly successful investment manager who owned a portfolio of "blue-chip" securities valued at more than $130 million.
He was able to get about $24.55 million in loans and other credits from Chemical Bank from 1992 through 1994 by allegedly lying about the value of his securities and cash holdings.
White allegedly assisted in the scheme by wrongfully verifying that Deloitte had confirmed Bagdasarian's holdings.
The men vastly overstated the value of Bagdasarian's portfolio, claiming that it reached more than $521 million, prosecutors alleged.

In the second part of the alleged scheme, Bagdasarian approached Salomon seeking its assistance in raising capital for Normandy America. Salomon, along with Alex. Brown Inc and Schroder Wertheim & Co, agreed to underwrite the $196.4 million initial public offering and a $20.6 million private placement.
The complaint alleges that in August 1994 he falsely represented to Salomon that he had achieved multi-year returns of about 30 percent per year on about $700 million in assets under his management.
Bagdasarian and White allegedly represented that the securities were held in about 30 entities located outside the United States.
They resisted Salomon's request for details by claiming the structure of the offshore entities was created by and was proprietary to Deloitte.
